questions.problem:
Determine if $v=[\begin{aligned}1+\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 4 \\ -8 & 4\end{aligned}].$
If so, then what is the corresponding eigenvalue?
questions.worked_solution:
The eigenvectors are non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 4 \\ -8 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1+\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4-4\text{i} \\ -8\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4{\text{i}}^{2}-4\text{i} \\ -8\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =-4\text{i}[\begin{aligned}1+\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =-4\text{i}v.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Av=-4\text{i}v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =-4\text{i}.$

questions.problem:
Determine if $v=[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].$
If so, then what is the corresponding eigenvalue?
questions.worked_solution:
The eigenvectors are non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 1+\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-{\text{i}}^{2}-\text{i} \\ 1+\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\text{i}(\text{i}+1) \\ 1+\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =(1+\text{i})[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =(1+\text{i})v.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Av=(1+\text{i})v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =1+\text{i}.$

questions.problem:
If $v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of 
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -4 & -1\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =\sqrt{3}\text{i},$
then what is the value of $\frac{b}{a}?$
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =\sqrt{3}\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -4 & -1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3}\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{3}\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1-\sqrt{3}\text{i} & 1 \\ -4 & -1-\sqrt{3}\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(1-\sqrt{3}\text{i}){x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=0 \\ -4{x}_{1}+(-1-\sqrt{3}\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-\sqrt{3}\text{i}I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=-(1-\sqrt{3}\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ -(1-\sqrt{3}\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=-1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1-\sqrt{3}\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{b}{a}=\frac{1-\sqrt{3}\text{i}}{-1}=\sqrt{3}\text{i}-1.$

$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(2+3\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. $$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}(1+3\text{i}){x}_{2}

$$

questions.problem:
Given that ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ are linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}7 & 5 \\ -4 & 3\end{aligned}],$
what is the value of $\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we must solve the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}7-\lambda  & 5 \\ -4 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (7-\lambda )(3-\lambda )-(-4)(5) & =0 \\ 21-7\lambda -3\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}+20 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +41 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a} \\  & =\frac{10\pm \sqrt{(-10)^{2}-4(1)(41)}}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{10\pm \sqrt{-64}}{2} \\  & =\frac{10\pm 8\text{i}}{2} \\  & =5\pm 4\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are $\lambda =5\pm 4\text{i}.$

Now, let's consider the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=5+4\text{i}.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 5 \\ -4 & 3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}5+4\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 5+4\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2-4\text{i} & 5 \\ -4 & -2-4\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we get the system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(2-4\text{i}){x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=0 \\ -4{x}_{1}+(-2-4\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(5+4\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=(-\frac{2}{5}+\frac{4}{5}\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ (-\frac{2}{5}+\frac{4}{5}\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=5,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -2+4\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Then, to compute the second eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=5-4\text{i}$, we simply compute the complex conjugate of ${\overset{―}{v}}_{1},$ and get

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -2-4\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}} & =\frac{(5)(5)}{(-2+4\text{i})(-2-4\text{i})}=\frac{5}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Let ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ be linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -5 \\ 10 & 6\end{aligned}].$
Given that ${\lambda }_{1}=1+5\text{i}$ is an eigenvalue of $A,$ find the value of $\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,{\lambda }_{1}=1+5\text{i}$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & -5 \\ 10 & 6\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1+5\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 1+5\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5-5\text{i} & -5 \\ 10 & 5-5\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(-5-5\text{i}){x}_{1}-5{x}_{2}=0 \\ 10{x}_{1}+(5-5\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(1+5\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}(1-\text{i}){x}_{2}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}(1-\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-2,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

On the other hand, since ${\lambda }_{1}=1+5\text{i}$ is a complex eigenvalue of $A,$ the second eigenvalue of $A$ must be the complex conjugate of ${\lambda }_{1}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\lambda }_{2}=\overset{―}{{\lambda }_{1}}=1-5\text{i}.
$$

Moreover, the corresponding eigenvector to ${\lambda }_{2}$ is

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1+\text{i} \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}=\frac{(1-\text{i})(1+\text{i})}{(-2)(-2)}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a} \\  & =\frac{-(-2)\pm \sqrt{(-2)^{2}-4(1)(10)}}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{-(-2)\pm \sqrt{-36}}{2} \\  & =\frac{2\pm 6\text{i}}{2} \\  & =1\pm 3\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are $\lambda =1\pm 3\text{i}.$

Now, let's consider the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=1+3\text{i}.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 5 \\ -5 & -3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1+3\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 1+3\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4-3\text{i} & 5 \\ -5 & -4-3\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we get the system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(4-3\text{i}){x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=0 \\ -5{x}_{1}+(-4-3\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(1+3\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{5}(-4-3\text{i}){x}_{2}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}(-4-3\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-5,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4+3\text{i} \\ -5\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Then, to compute the second eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=1-3\text{i}$, we simply compute the complex conjugate of ${\overset{―}{v}}_{1},$ and get

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4-3\text{i} \\ -5\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}} & =\frac{(-5)(-5)}{(4+3\text{i})(4-3\text{i})}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given that ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ are linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}],$
what is the value of $\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we must solve the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-6-\lambda  & -4 \\ 5 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-6-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-(-4)(5) & =0 \\ -12+6\lambda -2\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}+20 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +8 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a} \\  & =\frac{-4\pm \sqrt{{4}^{2}-4(1)(8)}}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{-4\pm 4\text{i}}{2} \\  & =-2\pm 2\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are $\lambda =-2\pm 2\text{i}.$

Now, let's consider the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-2+2\text{i}.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-2+2\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -2+2\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4-2\text{i} & -4 \\ 5 & 4-2\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we get the system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(-4-2\text{i}){x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}=0 \\ 5{x}_{1}+(4-2\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(-2+2\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=(-1-\frac{1}{2}\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ (-1-\frac{1}{2}\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=2,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2-\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Then, to compute the second eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-2-2\text{i}$, we simply compute the complex conjugate of ${\overset{―}{v}}_{1},$ and get

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2+\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}} & =\frac{(2)(2)}{(-2-\text{i})(-2+\text{i})}=\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:

If so, then what is the corresponding eigenvalue?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $\mathbf{v}$ such that $A\mathbf{v}=\lambda \mathbf{v}.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 \\ 8 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1+3\text{i} \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-18+6\text{i} \\ 24\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}18{\text{i}}^{2}+6\text{i} \\ 24\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =6\text{i}[\begin{aligned}1+3\text{i} \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =6\text{i}v.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A\mathbf{v} = 6\textrm{i} \mathbf{v},$ we conclude that $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda=6\textrm{i}.$

$$

In our case, we have $\,\lambda_1 =4+5\textrm{i}$ and

$$

$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}-5\text{i}{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=0 \\ -5{x}_{1}-5\text{i}{x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(4+5\textrm{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another.

As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
x_2 = \textrm{i}x_1.
$$

So, the general solution is given by
